historical_timeline.summary: Father died, at about the time she turned six.
Back injured in a train collision in North Carolina.
Severely injured in an automobile accident in Florida.
Moved back to Darke County, Ohio, in declining health.
Died in Greenville, Ohio; pernicious anemia reported as the cause.

claims.statement: Annie Oakley was born Phoebe Ann Moses (also spelled Mosey) on August 13, 1860, in Darke County, Ohio, to Jacob Moses and Susan Wise Moses.
Her father died when she was six; two sources give pneumonia as the cause, and the Garst Museum says he died from exposure to winter weather. Her mother was left to support a large family.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Pneumonia after winter exposure, as reported; no further detail is recorded.

claims.statement: She became a celebrated exhibition sharpshooter who toured with a Wild West show in the United States and Europe, and in later years she gave exhibitions and taught women to shoot.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents her occupation; used for the synthetic social history.

claims.statement: On October 29, 1901, the show's train collided head-on with another train in North Carolina; Oakley's back was injured, and the accident ended her touring with the show.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The back injury is documented; its nature, and any treatment, are reported inconsistently and are not used.

source_links.locator: Date and place of the collision

claims.statement: Late in 1922 she was severely injured in an automobile accident in Florida, reported as fractures of the hip and ankle, after which she had to wear a brace on her leg; her recovery took more than a year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The accident and long recovery are documented in two sources; the fractures and brace are reported in one.

source_links.locator: Accident and recovery of more than a year
Florida, hip and ankle fractures, brace

claims.statement: Her health declined in the years after the accident, and in 1925 she moved back to Darke County, Ohio.
Oakley died on November 3, 1926, in Greenville, Ohio, aged 66; the Garst Museum and HistoryNet give pernicious anemia as the cause of death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic pernicious anemia episode. How the diagnosis was made in 1926 is not recorded in the cited sources. Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Diagnose pernicious anemia with early neurologic involvement in a slight, active woman of 64; replace B12 by injection and confirm the response on the CMID schedule; stage autoimmune gastritis by endoscopy for gastric neoplasia and neuroendocrine tumors; recognize the iron deficiency that recovery unmasks; and manage chronic low back pain from old injuries with exercise-first ACP care while checking neuropathy and fall risk.

hpi.narrative: Mrs. Oakley returns one week after starting intramuscular cyanocobalamin for pernicious anemia. The practice nurse gave all seven daily injections. Her tongue is less sore and she has a little more energy, though she is still breathless on one flight of stairs. The tingling in both feet is unchanged, and she still feels unsteady in the dark. She has had no palpitations, muscle cramps, or leg swelling. She began physical therapy for her back five days ago and has done her home exercises daily. She saw Dr. Salib of hematology this morning.

referral.question: Macrocytic anemia with mild leukopenia and thrombocytopenia in a woman of 64, with very low B12, raised MMA, and positive intrinsic factor antibodies. Please confirm pernicious anemia and advise on replacement, monitoring, and gastric risk
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks; B12 injections start tomorrow
referral.pertinent_history: Four months of tiredness, breathlessness on one flight of stairs, a sore tongue, tingling in both feet, and unsteadiness in the dark. Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, MCV 114 fL, white cells 3.6, platelets 128, reticulocytes 0.6 percent. B12 96 pg/mL, folate 11.8 ng/mL, MMA 2.10 micromol/L, intrinsic factor antibody 38.4 AU/mL. LDH 612 U/L and bilirubin 1.6 mg/dL. Ferritin 52 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 34 percent, TSH 2.1, potassium 4.1, eGFR 93. Examination: smooth red tongue, absent vibration at the toes, reduced proprioception, positive Romberg. She eats meat and dairy daily, takes no metformin or acid suppressants, and has had no gastric surgery. Chronic low back pain from old injuries; physical therapy is starting
questions: Do these results establish pernicious anemia, and do the low white cell and platelet counts or the raised LDH need a bone marrow examination or a hemolysis work-up?
Which replacement schedule do you advise with these neurologic findings, and is oral B12 an option for her?
Which tests should confirm the response, and when? Should the B12 level be repeated?
What gastric evaluation is needed for gastric cancer and neuroendocrine tumor risk, and how often?
What else should we watch for, such as iron deficiency, potassium, or thyroid disease?

consultant_note.history: Mrs. Oakley is seen at the request of Dr. Ellingsen one week after starting intramuscular cyanocobalamin for macrocytic anemia with low B12 and positive intrinsic factor antibodies. She has had all seven daily injections. Her tongue is less sore and her energy slightly better; the foot tingling and unsteadiness in the dark are unchanged. She has no bleeding, bruising, fevers, weight loss, or night sweats. No alcohol excess, nitrous oxide exposure, metformin, or acid suppressants. She teaches shooting classes and wants to keep doing so
consultant_note.data_reviewed: The presenting blood count, reticulocytes, B12, folate, MMA, intrinsic factor antibody, LDH, bilirubin, iron studies, TSH, and kidney function; today's blood count, reticulocyte count of 6.8 percent, and potassium of 3.7 mmol/L

exam.finding: Slight, pale, alert
Smooth, red tongue, less inflamed
No lymph node enlargement; spleen not palpable
Vibration absent at the toes and reduced at the ankles; proprioception reduced at the toes; Romberg positive; cognition normal

assessment.display: Pernicious anemia with B12 deficiency neuropathy
assessment.assessment: Established. Very low B12 with raised MMA confirms deficiency, and intrinsic factor antibodies are highly specific for pernicious anemia. The mild leukopenia and thrombocytopenia, raised LDH, and raised bilirubin come from ineffective red cell production in the marrow. The reticulocyte rise to 6.8 percent at one week, with counts already climbing, confirms the diagnosis. A bone marrow examination is not needed unless the counts fail to normalize by eight weeks. The neurologic signs show dorsal column involvement, so treatment must be by injection and must not lapse
Pernicious anemia is the late stage of autoimmune gastritis, which raises the risk of type 1 gastric neuroendocrine tumors and gastric adenocarcinoma. She has never had an endoscopy

Autoimmune thyroid disease is common with autoimmune gastritis; her TSH is normal. Iron deficiency often appears as red cell production recovers, because absorption of dietary iron is reduced without gastric acid

recommendations: Continue cyanocobalamin 1000 micrograms intramuscularly: weekly for four weeks after the daily week, then monthly for life. Oral B12 is not advised for her while neurologic signs are present, and injections should never be stopped
If neurologic signs stop improving or symptoms return before each monthly dose, shorten the interval
Blood count with MCV and MMA at eight weeks; do not repeat the B12 level
Ferritin and transferrin saturation at eight weeks; if iron deficiency appears, treat it and complete the GI evaluation

Upper endoscopy with biopsies of the gastric body and antrum in separate jars, of any polyp or nodule, and of the duodenum, with H. pylori testing. Surveillance after that by the findings: about every three years for advanced atrophy, every one to two years if neuroendocrine tumors are found
Avoid nitrous oxide anesthesia, which inactivates B12
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Ellingsen today; the patient agrees and has the plan in writing
consultant_note.follow_up: Hematology will see her again if the blood counts do not normalize by eight weeks or if new cytopenias appear. Primary care continues the injections and monitoring on the CMID schedule
